content: The guideline development process involved several critical steps to ensure a robust and evidence-based approach. The steering group meticulously outlined the scope of the guideline and formulated key questions using the PICO (Population, Intervention, Comparison, Outcome) format. They identified a systematic review team and a guideline methodologist, finalized a detailed planning proposal, and facilitated the selection of the guideline development group and external resource experts. The group supervised the retrieval, assessment, and synthesis of evidence, collected and evaluated disclosures of interest, and managed conflicts of interest in consultation with the Office of Compliance, Risk Management, and Ethics. The steering group drafted recommendations based on the decisions of the guideline development group, prepared the final guideline document, managed the peer-review process, and oversaw the dissemination of the guideline. Regional advisors from WHO regions actively participated in the meetings of the guideline development group. The guideline development group was formed by selecting candidates from WHO advisors and experts, a call for expressions of interest, recommendations from other WHO departments, and literature reviews. Out of 20 individuals approached, 18 expressed interest and submitted their curriculum vitae and declarations of interest. The group, comprising 18 members with expertise in epidemiology, nutrition, maternal and infant health care, pediatrics, and systematic reviews, included 13 women and 5 men representing all six WHO regions. The group scoped the guideline, drafted key questions in PICO format, and prioritized outcomes during a meeting held on May 11–12, 2017. In a subsequent meeting on June 26–28, 2018, they reviewed and appraised the evidence using GRADE (Grading of Recommendations, Assessment, Development, and Evaluation) evidence profiles. They interpreted the evidence using the DECIDE framework, which considers intervention effects, evidence quality, values, preferences, resources, equity, acceptability, and feasibility to guide recommendation formulation. The systematic review team, including groups from the University of Dundee and Johns Hopkins School of Public Health, conducted comprehensive reviews to address the key questions identified. These reviews synthesized evidence for critical health outcomes related to breastfeeding counseling and were presented at the guideline development group meeting in Geneva in June 2018. The quality of evidence was assessed using the GRADE approach, with outcomes rated as high, moderate, low, or very low based on criteria such as risk of bias, inconsistency, imprecision, indirectness, and publication bias. The steering group managed potential conflicts of interest in compliance with WHO guidelines. All guideline development group members completed standard WHO declaration-of-interest and confidentiality forms and submitted updated curriculum vitae. Publicly available information was reviewed to identify any intellectual biases or positions held by prospective members. Concerns were discussed with the WHO Office of Compliance, Risk Management, and Ethics, and conflicts of interest were managed on a case-by-case basis. Members with no perceived or real conflicts of interest were asked to declare their research and funding sources verbally. The guideline development group evaluated the balance of benefits and harms, considering the magnitude and importance of effects. Recommendations were categorized as recommended, context-specific recommendation, or not recommended. Context-specific recommendations were made when regional differences in feasibility or resource use impacted implementation. The group also reviewed qualitative information on values, preferences, and acceptability among stakeholders, including pregnant women, mothers, and healthcare providers. Strategies to address concerns about acceptability during implementation were discussed when necessary. Resource implications were evaluated to determine the cost-effectiveness and resource intensity of the intervention in different settings. Recommendations were informed by systematic reviews, GRADE evidence profiles, and an evidence-to-decision framework. The overall quality of evidence, as presented in the GRADE profiles, was a key factor in drafting recommendations. High-quality evidence across critical outcomes increased the likelihood of a clear positive recommendation, while low-quality evidence often warranted context-specific recommendations.
